entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be forgotten by someone, usually by accident and only for a while.
entries.usage: A common, polite way to admit you forgot something: *Sorry, it completely slipped my mind.* The forgotten thing is the subject and the person is the possessive: *The meeting slipped her mind.* It sounds softer than *I forgot*, so it's useful in apologies at work.
examples: I'm so sorry I didn't call you back — it completely **slipped my mind**.
Their anniversary **slipped his mind**, and she still hasn't let him forget it.
The dentist appointment must have **slipped Dad's mind**, because he went golfing instead.

drill.sentence: I meant to pay the electric bill on Friday, but it {{slipped my mind}}, and now there's a late fee.
drill.hint: was accidentally forgotten (not *went out of my head*)

entries.related: *go out of your head* — be forgotten, informal; *on the tip of your tongue* — almost remembered but not quite; *forget* — plain.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be unable to remember something, or to fail to find any answer or information.
entries.usage: Common in conversation when your memory suddenly fails: *I drew a blank on her name.* It's also used for searches that find nothing: *Detectives drew a blank.* Americans also say simply *I blanked* or *My mind went blank*.
examples: I recognized his face, but when I tried to introduce him, I **drew a blank** on his name.
When the teacher called on me, I completely **drew a blank**.
Detectives **drew a blank** when they checked the hotel's guest records.

drill.sentence: Someone asked me for the Wi-Fi password at my own house, and I totally {{drew a blank}}.
drill.hint: suddenly couldn't remember — the three-word form (not *blanked*)

entries.related: *my mind went blank* — I suddenly couldn't think; *come up empty* — find nothing; *slip your mind* — be forgotten.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start to make sense, or to start working out well after a period of confusion or difficulty.
entries.usage: Used about plans, careers and mysteries: *Everything fell into place.* It often describes success that seems to happen naturally once a key problem is solved, or the moment a puzzle suddenly makes sense. The subject is usually *things*, *everything* or *the pieces*.
examples: Once I found an apartment near the office, everything else **fell into place**.
When the detective learned about the second key, the whole story **fell into place**.
After a rough first year, things finally **fell into place** for the young band.

drill.sentence: We were stressed about the wedding for months, but in the last few weeks everything just {{fell into place}}.
drill.hint: went smoothly, as if each piece found its spot (not *came together*)

entries.related: *come together* — start to work well as a whole; *work out* — end successfully; *click* — suddenly become clear, informal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: From the very beginning, without using anything that already exists, such as a ready-made mix or earlier work.
entries.usage: Very common in cooking (*a cake from scratch* means not from a mix), building, writing and business: *start from scratch*, *build something from scratch*. It stresses starting with nothing. *From the ground up* is close but stresses building every level, often with pride.
entries.pattern: start / make / build something from scratch
examples: My grandmother never used a mix; she made every cake **from scratch**.
After the fire, the family had to rebuild their lives **from scratch**.
We decided to rewrite the app **from scratch** instead of patching the old code.

drill.sentence: This pizza dough isn't from the store; I made it {{from scratch}} this morning.
drill.hint: starting with basic ingredients, no mix

entries.related: *from the ground up* — completely, starting at the base; *start over* — begin again; *reinvent the wheel* — waste time creating something that already exists.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Completely, starting from the most basic level, as when you build something new or rebuild it totally.
entries.usage: Used about building companies, products and buildings, and about learning a trade: *build a business from the ground up*, *redesigned from the ground up*. Compared with *from scratch*, it stresses that every level was built, often with pride in the effort. It's common in business writing and ads.
examples: My parents built their restaurant **from the ground up**, starting with a food cart.
The new pickup truck has been redesigned **from the ground up**.
She learned the hotel business **from the ground up**, starting as a housekeeper.

drill.sentence: The new owners didn't just repaint the old diner; they rebuilt the business {{from the ground up}}, with a new menu, new staff and a new name.
drill.hint: completely, starting at the foundation (not *from scratch*)

entries.related: *from scratch* — from nothing, without existing material; *top to bottom* — completely and thoroughly; *start at the bottom* — begin a career in the lowest job.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation or relationship in which both sides must give, take and make an effort.
entries.usage: Used to remind someone that respect, trust, communication or loyalty must go both ways: *Respect is a two-way street.* It's neutral and common at work, in families and in relationships. The subject is often an abstract noun like *trust* or *communication*.
examples: Trust is **a two-way street**; if you want me to trust you, stop reading my messages.
Good mentoring is **a two-way street** — I learn as much from my students as they learn from me.
Loyalty is **a two-way street**, and the company showed none when it cut our pensions.

drill.sentence: I'm happy to cover your shifts, but this is {{a two-way street}} — next time I need help, I expect you to step in.
drill.hint: something both sides must contribute to (a traffic image)

entries.related: *give and take* — willingness to compromise; *it takes two to tango* — both people are responsible; *a one-way street* — a relationship in which only one side gives.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An action that insults or upsets someone, especially because it shows no respect for them or their efforts.
entries.usage: Used about decisions, offers and remarks that feel insulting: *A one percent raise after the year we had is a slap in the face.* It's emotional and strong, and common in conversation and news. Typical frames are *feel like a slap in the face* and *a slap in the face to someone*.
entries.pattern: be / feel like a slap in the face (to someone)
examples: After ten years with the company, being replaced by an intern felt like **a slap in the face**.
The tiny raise was **a slap in the face** to nurses who had worked double shifts all winter.
It was **a slap in the face** when my brother sold Dad's old guitar without even asking me.

drill.sentence: The city closed our neighborhood library and opened a parking garage in its place, which residents called {{a slap in the face}}.
drill.hint: an insulting act — an open-hand image (not *a kick in the teeth* or *a low blow*)

entries.related: *a kick in the teeth* — a cruel disappointment, stronger; *add insult to injury* — make a bad situation even worse; *a backhanded compliment* — praise that is really an insult.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A small, harmless lie told to be polite or to avoid hurting someone's feelings.
entries.usage: Very common, often used to admit or excuse a small untruth: *I told a little white lie.* *Little* is often added, and the usual verb is *tell*. It's seen as socially acceptable, unlike a real lie, and is used about gifts, food, excuses and compliments.
examples: I told **a white lie** and said I loved the sweater my aunt knitted for me.
Saying you're five minutes away when you're still at home is a classic **white lie**.
Most parents tell a few **white lies** — about the tooth fairy, for example.

drill.sentence: When my friend asked if I liked her new haircut, I told {{a white lie}} and said it looked great.
drill.hint: a small polite untruth — a color image (not *a fib*)

entries.related: *a fib* — a small, unimportant lie, informal; *a half-truth* — a statement that is partly true but misleading; *bend the truth* — say something not completely true.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who likes to stay up late and is most active at night.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk, often used about yourself: *I'm a night owl.* The opposite is *an early bird* or *a morning person*. It's friendly, not critical, and it's often used to explain someone's schedule.
examples: I'm **a night owl**, so early meetings are torture for me.
The diner stays open until three in the morning for the city's **night owls**.
Ever since college, Priya has been **a night owl**; she does her best painting after midnight.

drill.sentence: My teenage son is {{a night owl}}; he's wide awake at midnight and impossible to wake before ten.
drill.hint: someone who stays up late — a bird image

entries.related: *an early bird* — someone who gets up early; *a morning person* — someone who feels best in the morning; *burn the midnight oil* — work late into the night.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person used to test something new, such as a product, a method or a treatment.
entries.usage: Often used humorously about yourself or people close to you: *You're my guinea pig for this recipe.* It can also be a complaint about being tested on without agreement: *We're not guinea pigs!* It usually follows *be*, *act as* or *use someone as*.
examples: My roommate was my **guinea pig** for the new curry recipe, and he survived.
Volunteers in the clinical trial agreed to act as **guinea pigs** for a new migraine drug.
Parents complained that their kids were being used as **guinea pigs** for an untested math curriculum.

drill.sentence: I'm not sure about this new hair dye. Will you be my {{guinea pig}} and try it first?
drill.hint: the person who tests it first — an animal image (not *test subject*)

entries.related: *a test subject* — a person in an experiment, more neutral; *a trial run* — a test before the real thing; *a lab rat* — a similar image, more negative.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very high, usually after rising quickly; used about prices, levels or demand.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news about prices, rents, costs and emotions: *Rents have gone through the roof.* It usually follows *go* or *be*. With a person as the subject, *go through the roof* can also mean to get very angry, like *hit the roof*.
examples: Rents in our neighborhood have gone **through the roof** since the new subway line opened.
Ticket sales went **through the roof** after the band played on late-night TV.
The kids' excitement was **through the roof** on Christmas morning.

drill.sentence: After a storm destroyed half the orange crop, juice prices went {{through the roof}}.
drill.hint: rose to a very high level — a house image (not *sky-high*)

entries.related: *off the charts* — extremely high, beyond the normal range; *skyrocket* — rise very quickly (verb); *hit the roof* — become very angry.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: By trying different methods and learning from mistakes until you find one that works.
entries.usage: Common in talk about learning skills, cooking, fixing things and research: *I learned to bake bread by trial and error.* It suggests a practical approach without instructions or theory. *Through trial and error* is just as common, and *trial-and-error* works as an adjective: *a trial-and-error approach*.
examples: Nobody taught me to fix bikes; I figured it out **by trial and error**.
The lab found the right temperature **by trial and error**, after dozens of failed attempts.
After years of **trial and error**, my mom finally has the perfect pie crust recipe.

drill.sentence: There were no instructions with the old sewing machine, so I learned how to thread it {{by trial and error}}.
drill.hint: by experimenting and learning from failures (the form with *by*, not *through*)

entries.related: *learn the hard way* — learn from a painful experience; *hit or miss* — not reliable; *figure something out* — find the answer by thinking or trying.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Directly from the person who knows the facts best, usually the person involved.
entries.usage: Used to stress that information is reliable because it comes from the source itself, not from rumors. It's informal and often humorous. Common frames are *hear it straight from the horse's mouth* and *get it straight from the horse's mouth*.
entries.pattern: hear / get something straight from the horse's mouth
examples: I didn't believe the rumor until I got it **straight from the horse's mouth**: the owner told me the diner is closing in June.
Fans got the news **straight from the horse's mouth** when the singer announced her retirement on her own podcast.
Don't trust what you read online about the new bus routes; get it **straight from the horse's mouth** at the city's public meeting.

drill.sentence: My son says his teacher canceled the homework, but I'd rather hear it {{straight from the horse's mouth}}.
drill.hint: directly from the person who knows (an animal image)

entries.related: *firsthand* — from your own experience; *from a reliable source* — plain; *hearsay* — information heard from others that may not be true.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extremely happy and pleased about something.
entries.usage: Very common in British English and widely used by Americans too, especially about good news such as a birth, a new job or a win: *We're over the moon.* It's informal and warm. It usually follows *be* and often takes *about* or *with*.
entries.pattern: be over the moon (about / with something)
examples: My parents are **over the moon** about becoming grandparents.
She was **over the moon** when she got into her first-choice college.
Our neighbors were **over the moon** when their son came home from Japan for the holidays.

drill.sentence: When the shelter called to say we could adopt the puppy, my kids were {{over the moon}}.
drill.hint: extremely happy — an image of jumping very high (not *on cloud nine*)

entries.related: *on cloud nine* — extremely happy, more common in American English; *walking on air* — very happy; *thrilled* — plain.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop yourself from laughing or showing what you really feel, even though something is funny.
entries.usage: Usually about trying not to laugh at a serious moment: *I could hardly keep a straight face.* It's often negative or used with *try to* or *manage to*. It can also mean hiding the truth while telling a joke or a lie.
examples: When the boss's dog started snoring loudly during the video call, nobody could **keep a straight face**.
My dad told the kids that broccoli was "tiny trees for giants" and somehow **kept a straight face**.
It's hard to **keep a straight face** when your toddler explains why the cat is wearing your socks.

drill.sentence: During the wedding vows, the groom's voice cracked like a teenager's, and I struggled to {{keep a straight face}}.
drill.hint: avoid laughing and look serious

entries.related: *crack up* — start laughing; *a poker face* — a face that shows no emotion; *keep your composure* — stay calm, more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The member of a family or group who is seen as different from the others, often as a disappointment or an embarrassment.
entries.usage: Usually *the black sheep of the family*, often said about yourself with humor or even pride. It can be mild teasing or a serious judgment. It can also describe one bad member of a group or an industry.
entries.pattern: the black sheep of the family / of a group
examples: My uncle is **the black sheep** of the family; nobody knows exactly what he does for a living.
In a family of doctors, I was **the black sheep** because I wanted to be a musician.
The airline was long seen as **the black sheep** of the industry because of its lost bags and rude staff.

drill.sentence: Everyone in my family went to law school except my cousin Ray, who dropped out to surf in Hawaii; he's always been {{the black sheep}}.
drill.hint: the family's disappointment — an animal image (not *the odd one out*)

entries.related: *the odd one out* — the one who is different, not necessarily bad; *a bad apple* — one bad person who harms a group; *a rebel* — someone who rejects the rules.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To spend less money than before because you have less or because times are hard.
entries.usage: Used about families, companies and governments cutting costs: *We'll have to tighten our belts this year.* It's neutral and common in news about budgets and in family talk. The possessive changes, and *belt-tightening* is a common noun.
examples: After my wife lost her job, we had to **tighten our belts** and cancel our summer vacation.
With fuel prices up, airlines are **tightening their belts** and cutting routes.
The school district will have to **tighten its belt** after the state cut its funding.

drill.sentence: With a new baby and only one income, we're going to have to {{tighten our belts}} for a while.
drill.hint: spend less money — a clothing image (not *cut back*)

entries.related: *cut back* — reduce spending or use; *make ends meet* — have just enough money to live; *pinch pennies* — be very careful with money.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: At the last possible moment, just before it is too late.
entries.usage: Common in news about deals, rescues and decisions: *The strike was avoided at the eleventh hour.* It's neutral to slightly formal. Before a noun it takes a hyphen: *an eleventh-hour deal*.
examples: The two sides reached a deal **at the eleventh hour**, and the strike was called off.
My brother always writes his best-man speeches **at the eleventh hour**, usually the night before the wedding.
The music festival was saved **at the eleventh hour** when a new sponsor stepped in.

drill.sentence: Our flight was canceled, but {{at the eleventh hour}} the airline found us two seats on another plane.
drill.hint: at the very last moment — a clock image (not *at the last minute* or *in the nick of time*)

entries.related: *at the last minute* — same, more casual; *in the nick of time* — just in time; *down to the wire* — until the very end.
entries.origin: From the Bible's parable of the workers in the vineyard, where the last workers are hired at the eleventh hour of a twelve-hour working day.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To fail suddenly, completely and often very publicly.
entries.usage: Informal and dramatic, used about plans, businesses, relationships, sports teams and proposals: *The deal went down in flames.* It suggests a spectacular failure, not a quiet one. The image is of a burning plane falling from the sky.
examples: His plan to open a second restaurant **went down in flames** when the bank pulled the loan.
The team was undefeated all season, then **went down in flames** in the first playoff game.
My attempt to impress her with my cooking **went down in flames** when I found out she's allergic to shrimp.

drill.sentence: The proposal to build a casino near the lake {{went down in flames}} after hundreds of residents showed up to oppose it.
drill.hint: failed completely and publicly (not *crashed and burned*)

entries.related: *crash and burn* — fail badly, very similar; *fall flat* — fail to have the intended effect; *a flop* — a failure, especially a show or a product.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very rare; not found or happening often.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about things that are hard to find, such as good jobs, gas stations or quiet moments: *Good plumbers are few and far between.* It usually follows *be* or *become*. The form is fixed.
examples: On this stretch of highway, gas stations are **few and far between**.
Days off have been **few and far between** since I started this job.
Her visits home became **few and far between** after she moved to Alaska.

drill.sentence: Honest used-car dealers are {{few and far between}}, so have any car checked by a mechanic before you buy it.
drill.hint: very rare — a phrase about numbers and distance

entries.related: *scarce* — not enough of something; *once in a blue moon* — very rarely; *a dime a dozen* — very common, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To accept the unpleasant results of something you did, such as criticism or punishment.
entries.usage: Used when someone must deal with the consequences of a mistake or wrongdoing: *It's time to face the music.* It's neutral and common with parents and kids, at work and in news. It suggests that the person can no longer avoid it.
examples: I broke Mom's favorite vase, and now I have to go home and **face the music**.
After the accounting scandal broke, the company's CEO had to **face the music** at a packed press conference.
You can't hide from your credit card bills forever; at some point you'll have to **face the music**.

drill.sentence: He skipped three weeks of piano lessons without telling his parents, and now he has to {{face the music}}.
drill.hint: accept the unpleasant consequences (not *own up*)

entries.related: *own up* — admit you did something wrong; *take the heat* — accept criticism; *pay the price* — suffer as a result of your actions.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: So near, in distance, time or result, that it makes you worried or uncomfortable.
entries.usage: Used about near accidents, close scores, tight deadlines and other things that nearly went wrong. It's neutral and very common, and *a little* or *a bit* is often added in front. It often follows *come*, *get* or *be*.
examples: A bear came a little **too close for comfort** while we were cooking dinner at the campsite.
We won, but a one-point lead with ten seconds left is **too close for comfort**.
The wildfire is now five miles from town — **too close for comfort** for many residents.

drill.sentence: A truck swerved into our lane and missed us by inches — way {{too close for comfort}}.
drill.hint: so near that it's frightening (the full four-word phrase)

entries.related: *a close call* — a near accident or failure; *cut it close* — leave very little time; *a near miss* — an accident that almost happened.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person, brand or product that almost everyone has heard of.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and business, usually as *become a household name*. It's positive about fame or success, and it's used for companies and products as well as people. *Not exactly a household name* is a polite way to say someone isn't famous.
examples: Twenty years ago she was an unknown singer from Tennessee; now she's **a household name**.
The tiny company became **a household name** after its video doorbell appeared on a popular TV show.
He's a great actor, but he's not exactly **a household name**.

drill.sentence: After his cooking show became a hit, the quiet baker from Ohio turned into {{a household name}} almost overnight.
drill.hint: someone nearly everybody knows (a home image; not *a celebrity*)

entries.related: *a celebrity* — a famous person; *a big name* — an important, well-known person; *put something on the map* — make something well known.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To change a situation so that you now have the advantage over someone who had it before.
entries.usage: Common in sports, competition, arguments and stories: *She turned the tables on her critics.* The usual pattern is *turn the tables on someone*. It's neutral and often describes a satisfying reversal.
examples: We lost to them badly in September, but we **turned the tables** in the rematch.
The scammer called pretending to be from my bank, so I **turned the tables** and started asking him questions.
In the movie's last act, the victim **turns the tables on** her kidnappers and escapes.

drill.sentence: My little sister always beats me at chess, but last night I finally {{turned the tables on}} her.
drill.hint: reversed the situation and beat (not *got even with*)

entries.related: *the shoe is on the other foot* — the situation is now reversed; *get even with someone* — take revenge; *turn the tide* — change the direction of a situation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that is very easy to do.
entries.usage: Very common and informal, often as a confident reply: *Piece of cake!* In short replies the *a* is usually dropped. It sounds relaxed, so avoid it in formal writing.
examples: The driving test was **a piece of cake**; I was done in ten minutes.
"Can you fix the leaky faucet?" "**Piece of cake**."
For a pro like her, a five-mile run is **a piece of cake**.

drill.sentence: After all that studying, the final exam was {{a piece of cake}}.
drill.hint: very easy — a dessert image (not *a breeze*)

entries.related: *a breeze* — very easy; *a walk in the park* — easy and pleasant; *easier said than done* — harder than it sounds, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The most basic, practical details of something, especially the ones that take real work to deal with.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, often as *get down to the nitty-gritty*, meaning to start dealing with the important details. It's informal and often contrasts with general ideas or small talk. It also works before a noun: *the nitty-gritty details*.
entries.pattern: get down to the nitty-gritty (of something)
examples: We agree on the general plan; now let's get down to **the nitty-gritty** of who does what.
The brochure looks nice, but I want **the nitty-gritty**: fees, contract length and cancellation rules.
My brother-in-law loves **the nitty-gritty** of restoring old cars — sanding, wiring and rebuilding engines.

drill.sentence: Our first meeting with the wedding planner was all ideas and colors; at the second, we finally got down to {{the nitty-gritty}}: budgets, seating charts and deadlines.
drill.hint: the basic practical details (a rhyming phrase; not *the nuts and bolts*)

entries.related: *the nuts and bolts* — the practical details of how something works; *the ins and outs* — all the details of a complex matter; *the big picture* — the overall view, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To learn news informally from other people, often as rumor or gossip, rather than from an official source.
entries.usage: Common at work and in communities, often when you don't want to say who told you: *I heard through the grapevine that you're leaving.* It's informal and neutral. The 1960s song *I Heard It Through the Grapevine* made the phrase even more familiar.
examples: I **heard through the grapevine** that Maria is getting promoted.
We **heard** about the store closing **through the grapevine** weeks before the official announcement.
News of their engagement got around **through the grapevine** before they'd even told their parents.

drill.sentence: Nobody told me officially, but I {{heard through the grapevine}} that our landlord is selling the building.
drill.hint: learned it unofficially from people talking (a plant image)

entries.related: *word of mouth* — information passed from person to person; *a little bird told me* — said playfully to hide your source; *the rumor mill* — the people and places where rumors spread.
entries.origin: From *the grapevine telegraph*, a 19th-century American term for news and rumors passed from person to person.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extremely happy and excited, usually because something good has just happened.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about engagements, new babies, big wins and new jobs: *She's been on cloud nine all week.* It's informal and slightly playful, and it usually follows *be* or *feel*. It means about the same as *over the moon*, which sounds a little more British.
examples: Ever since he got the job offer, Sam has been **on cloud nine**.
The newlyweds were still **on cloud nine** when they got back from their honeymoon.
Fans were **on cloud nine** after their team won its first championship in fifty years.

drill.sentence: My neighbor has been {{on cloud nine}} since he won two tickets to the World Series.
drill.hint: extremely happy — a weather image (not *over the moon*)

entries.related: *over the moon* — extremely happy, more British; *walking on air* — very happy; *in seventh heaven* — extremely happy, a little old-fashioned.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep something under control so that it doesn't grow, or to keep something secret.
entries.usage: Used about costs, emotions, problems and secrets: *keep a lid on spending*, *keep a lid on your temper*. It's informal and common at work and in news. For secrets, *keep a lid on it* means don't tell anyone yet.
entries.pattern: keep a lid on + costs / emotions / news
examples: The new manager is trying to **keep a lid on** costs by cutting overtime.
We're **keeping a lid on** the news until we've told both sets of parents.
Try to **keep a lid on** your temper at dinner, even if your uncle starts talking about money.

drill.sentence: Please {{keep a lid on}} the surprise party; Mom can't find out until Saturday.
drill.hint: say nothing about — a cooking-pot image

entries.related: *keep something under wraps* — keep something secret; *keep a cap on something* — limit an amount; *blow the lid off something* — reveal a secret or scandal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To ask someone to marry you.
entries.usage: Informal and cheerful, used in conversation and in news about engagements: *He finally popped the question.* It always means a marriage proposal, never other questions. The form is fixed; it's usually in the past tense or used to predict a proposal.
examples: After five years together, Mike finally **popped the question** on a beach in Maine.
She's sure he's going to **pop the question** on Valentine's Day.
My parents got engaged fast: Dad **popped the question** after only three dates.

drill.sentence: He hid the ring in her dessert and {{popped the question}} in front of the whole restaurant.
drill.hint: asked her to marry him (the informal phrase, not just *proposed*)

entries.related: *propose* — the neutral verb; *get engaged* — agree to marry; *tie the knot* — get married.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Money is limited and has to be earned, so you shouldn't waste it.
entries.usage: A classic thing parents say to children who ask for too much: *Money doesn't grow on trees, you know.* It's informal and often a bit scolding. Adults also use it about budgets at home or at work, often with humor.
examples: No, we're not buying another video game. **Money doesn't grow on trees**!
My dad's favorite line when I was a kid was "**Money doesn't grow on trees**."
The city council reminded residents that **money doesn't grow on trees** and the new pool would have to wait.

drill.sentence: Turn off the lights when you leave the room — {{money doesn't grow on trees}}, and the electric bill is huge.
drill.hint: cash is limited, so don't waste it (a garden image)

entries.related: *we're not made of money* — we can't afford everything; *there's no such thing as a free lunch* — nothing valuable is really free; *penny-pinching* — being very careful with money.

entries.term: at the drop of a hat
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Immediately and without hesitating, often without needing a good reason.
entries.usage: Used about people who act or react very quickly, sometimes too easily: *She'll cry at the drop of a hat.* It can be praise (*He'd help you at the drop of a hat*) or criticism. It usually comes at the end of the clause.
examples: My aunt would drive across the state **at the drop of a hat** to help any of us.
He changes his opinions **at the drop of a hat**, so it's hard to know what he really thinks.
Our toddler throws tantrums **at the drop of a hat**.

drill.sentence: Jenna loves travel so much that she'd pack a bag and fly to Tokyo {{at the drop of a hat}}.
drill.hint: instantly, with no hesitation — a clothing image (not *in a heartbeat*)

entries.related: *in a heartbeat* — immediately and gladly; *without a second thought* — without hesitating; *on a whim* — suddenly, for no good reason.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To fail, stop working or come to an end.
entries.usage: Informal and often humorous, used about machines, businesses, plans and teams: *My old laptop finally bit the dust.* It can also mean *to die*, a use familiar from old Western movies, which is why it sounds dramatic. It often comes with *finally*, or in the pattern *another one bites the dust*.
examples: Our twenty-year-old washing machine finally **bit the dust** last week.
Another bookstore on Main Street has **bitten the dust**.
My plans for a quiet weekend **bit the dust** when my in-laws called to say they were coming.

drill.sentence: After two hundred thousand miles, my old minivan finally {{bit the dust}} on the way to work.
drill.hint: stopped working for good — a Western-movie image (not *died* or *gave out*)

entries.related: *give up the ghost* — stop working, humorous; *go belly-up* — go bankrupt; *kick the bucket* — die, humorous.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very special; much better or kinder than almost anyone else.
entries.usage: Warm, sincere praise for people: *My mom is one in a million.* It's informal and often used to thank someone. The literal sense, *a one-in-a-million chance*, means something very unlikely.
examples: Thanks for driving me to the airport at four in the morning — you're **one in a million**.
Our family doctor was **one in a million**; she knew every patient's name and history.
A landlord who fixes things the same day you call is **one in a million**.

drill.sentence: My neighbor shoveled our driveway every morning while I was in the hospital. He's truly {{one in a million}}.
drill.hint: rare and wonderful — a phrase with a big number (not *a saint* or *one of a kind*)

entries.related: *a gem* — a very good person, informal; *one of a kind* — unique; *a keeper* — someone worth keeping, often a partner.

entries.term: take the bull by the horns
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal with a difficult situation directly, with courage and confidence, instead of avoiding it.
entries.usage: Used as encouragement or praise when someone faces a problem head-on: *I decided to take the bull by the horns and talk to my boss.* It's neutral and common at work and in personal life. The form is fixed.
examples: Instead of waiting for the landlord to call, I **took the bull by the horns** and went to his office.
If you want that promotion, you need to **take the bull by the horns** and ask for it.
The new principal **took the bull by the horns** and met with every angry parent in person.

drill.sentence: Our neighbors' dog had barked all night for weeks, so my wife {{took the bull by the horns}} and knocked on their door.
drill.hint: faced the problem directly and boldly (an animal image)

entries.related: *face something head-on* — deal with it directly; *grasp the nettle* — same, British; *bury your head in the sand* — ignore a problem, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that is very likely to succeed, be true or be a good choice.
entries.usage: Used for predictions and recommendations. Two patterns are common: *X is a safe bet* (a good choice) and *it's a safe bet that…* (a likely prediction). It's neutral and common in conversation, news and business.
entries.pattern: X is a safe bet; it's a safe bet that + clause
examples: If you don't know what wine to bring, a California cabernet is **a safe bet**.
It's **a safe bet** that the highway will be jammed on Thanksgiving weekend.
Investors see utility stocks as **a safe bet** when the economy slows down.

drill.sentence: If you're not sure what to get your nephew for his birthday, a gift card is always {{a safe bet}}.
drill.hint: a choice with almost no risk of going wrong — a gambling image (not *a sure bet*)

entries.related: *a sure thing* — something certain to happen; *a long shot* — something unlikely to succeed, the opposite; *play it safe* — avoid risks.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try to have the same possessions and lifestyle as your neighbors or friends, so that you don't seem less successful.
entries.usage: Usually critical or self-mocking, about spending money to impress people: *We're not trying to keep up with the Joneses.* It's common in talk about money, consumer culture and social media. *The Joneses* stands for any neighbors or peers and always takes *the*.
examples: Our neighbors bought a boat, a hot tub and a second SUV in one year; they're really trying to **keep up with the Joneses**.
Social media puts more pressure than ever on people to **keep up with the Joneses**.
We drive an old car and we're happy with it; we don't need to **keep up with the Joneses**.

drill.sentence: They bought a bigger house than they could afford just to {{keep up with the Joneses}}.
drill.hint: match the lifestyle of the neighbors (a family name)

entries.related: *a status symbol* — a thing people own to show their wealth; *live beyond your means* — spend more than you earn; *conspicuous consumption* — spending to show off, formal.
entries.origin: From the American comic strip *Keeping Up with the Joneses*, which started in 1913.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To change the direction in which a situation is developing, especially from bad to good.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and history writing: *The new treatment helped turn the tide against the disease.* It's neutral to slightly formal and often appears with *against* or *in someone's favor*. Without an object, people say *the tide has turned*.
entries.pattern: turn the tide (against something / in someone's favor)
examples: A goal just before halftime **turned the tide**, and we went on to win three to one.
The discovery of antibiotics **turned the tide** against many deadly infections.
Volunteers helped **turn the tide** in the fight to save the town's last movie theater.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood was in decline for years until a group of young families moved in and {{turned the tide}}.
drill.hint: reversed the trend — an ocean image

entries.related: *turn the tables* — reverse who has the advantage; *turn things around* — make a bad situation better; *a turning point* — the moment when things change.

entries.term: have the time of your life
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To enjoy yourself very much; to have one of the best experiences of your life.
entries.usage: Common and informal, used about trips, parties, concerts and childhood experiences: *The kids had the time of their lives.* The possessive matches the subject. It's warm and enthusiastic and usually in the past tense.
examples: The kids **had the time of their lives** at the water park.
We **had the time of our lives** backpacking through Italy after college.
My eighty-year-old neighbor **had the time of her life** on her first hot-air balloon ride.

drill.sentence: Thanks for inviting me on the fishing trip; I {{had the time of my life}}.
drill.hint: enjoyed it enormously (not *had a blast* or *had a ball*)

entries.related: *have a blast* — have a lot of fun, casual; *have a ball* — enjoy yourself very much; *a once-in-a-lifetime experience* — something you'll probably never do again.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The most basic parts or facts of something, without any details or extras.
entries.usage: Common as *the bare bones of a story / plan / agreement*. Before a noun it's hyphenated: *a bare-bones budget*, *a bare-bones apartment*, which suggests something cheap or minimal. It's neutral and fits both speech and writing.
entries.pattern: the bare bones of something; a bare-bones + noun
examples: Just give me **the bare bones** of the story; I don't need every detail.
The two sides have agreed on **the bare bones** of a deal, but the details could take months.
We stayed in a **bare-bones** cabin with no electricity or running water.

drill.sentence: I don't have time to read the whole contract, so can you tell me {{the bare bones}} — price, length and what happens if I cancel?
drill.hint: the most basic facts — a skeleton image (not *the gist*)

entries.related: *the gist* — the main idea; *the basics* — plain; *no-frills* — simple and without extras, about products and services.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A small mistake in speaking, when you say a word or name you didn't mean to say.
entries.usage: Used to excuse or explain a spoken mistake, often an embarrassing one: *Sorry, that was a slip of the tongue.* It's neutral. When the mistake seems to reveal a hidden thought, people call it a *Freudian slip*.
examples: I called my new boyfriend by my ex's name — **a slip of the tongue**, but he wasn't amused.
The announcer said "billion" instead of "million" and later apologized for **the slip of the tongue**.
It was just **a slip of the tongue** — I meant Tuesday, not Thursday.

drill.sentence: When I accidentally called my teacher "Mom" in front of the whole class, I blushed and said it was just {{a slip of the tongue}}.
drill.hint: an accidental spoken error (a mouth image)

entries.related: *a Freudian slip* — a mistake that seems to reveal a hidden thought; *misspeak* — say something wrong by accident, formal; *a typo* — a small mistake in writing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: So worried, frustrated or tired that you don't know what to do next.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and advice columns, about parents, caregivers and anyone with a problem they can't solve: *I'm at my wit's end with this baby.* It expresses real stress. The possessive changes (*at her wit's end*), and the spelling *wits' end* is also common.
examples: Our baby hasn't slept more than two hours at a time in weeks, and we're **at our wit's end**.
After three calls to customer service and still no refund, I was **at my wit's end**.
Teachers say they're **at their wit's end** with students using phones in class.

drill.sentence: My dog keeps escaping from the yard no matter what I try, and I'm {{at my wit's end}}.
drill.hint: so frustrated I don't know what to do (not *at the end of my rope*)

entries.related: *at the end of your rope* — same, very common in American English; *tearing your hair out* — very frustrated; *at a loss* — not sure what to do or say.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act calm and relaxed and not show strong interest, nervousness or excitement.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about dating, negotiating and job offers: *Just play it cool.* It suggests hiding eagerness on purpose. It's informal, and the *it* doesn't refer to anything specific.
examples: I really liked her, but I tried to **play it cool** and waited a day before texting back.
When the dealer offered a lower price, Dad **played it cool** and said he'd think about it.
The rookie **played it cool** in front of the cameras, but he admitted later that his hands were shaking.

drill.sentence: If the landlord sees how much you love the apartment, he might raise the rent, so {{play it cool}} during the tour.
drill.hint: act relaxed and hide how eager you are (not *act casual*)

entries.related: *act casual* — behave as if nothing special is happening; *keep your cool* — stay calm under pressure; *play hard to get* — pretend not to be interested, in dating.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop arguing or fighting and become friendly again.
entries.usage: Used about families, friends, rivals and businesses ending a long conflict: *The two brothers finally buried the hatchet.* It's neutral and slightly humorous, and it often comes with *finally*. *Bury the hatchet with someone* names the other side.
examples: After ten years of not speaking, my mom and her sister finally **buried the hatchet**.
The two rival coffee shops **buried the hatchet** and now run a charity event together every year.
It's time to **bury the hatchet** and focus on raising our kids together.

drill.sentence: The two neighbors fought over the fence for years, but they {{buried the hatchet}} after one helped the other during the flood.
drill.hint: ended their quarrel — a weapon image (not *made up*)

entries.related: *make up* — become friends again after an argument; *let bygones be bygones* — forget past problems; *mend fences* — repair a damaged relationship.
entries.origin: From a peace custom among some Native American peoples, described by European colonists in the 1600s, of burying weapons when a conflict ended.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To pay far too much money for something.
entries.usage: A common complaint about prices: *We paid through the nose for those tickets.* It's informal and is usually followed by *for*. It often suggests that you had little choice, as at an airport or in an emergency.
examples: If you buy a sandwich at the airport, you'll **pay through the nose**.
We **paid through the nose** for a hotel room because of the big game in town.
Without insurance, many patients **pay through the nose** for basic medicine.

drill.sentence: We forgot to book the ferry in advance, so we had to {{pay through the nose}} for last-minute tickets.
drill.hint: pay far too much — a face image

entries.related: *pay an arm and a leg* — pay a lot, very common; *a rip-off* — something that costs too much; *cost a fortune* — be very expensive.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which you have to do something very quickly, before a deadline or before it's too late.
entries.usage: Common in news about rescues, medical emergencies and construction, and in everyday talk about deadlines: *It's a race against time.* It sounds urgent and dramatic. *A race against the clock* is a common variant.
examples: Finding a kidney donor for her son became **a race against time**.
With the storm approaching, it was **a race against time** to get the boats out of the water.
Packing for the move turned into **a race against time** when the truck showed up three hours early.

drill.sentence: Rescuers knew it was {{a race against time}} to reach the hikers before the temperature dropped below freezing.
drill.hint: an urgent struggle to beat a deadline (not *… the clock*)

entries.related: *a race against the clock* — same; *down to the wire* — until the very last moment; *the clock is ticking* — time is running out.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A sudden success that does not last or is not repeated.
entries.usage: Used about artists, athletes, products and trends that look impressive at first: *Critics called her a flash in the pan.* It's neutral to critical and often appears in the negative: *not just a flash in the pan*. It suggests that the first success was luck.
examples: Critics called the young singer **a flash in the pan**, but her third album sold even better than her first.
Was the team's winning streak real, or just **a flash in the pan**?
The diet was everywhere for one summer and then disappeared — **a flash in the pan**.

drill.sentence: The restaurant was packed for its first month, but it turned out to be {{a flash in the pan}} and closed by spring.
drill.hint: a brief success that didn't last — a gunpowder image (not *a fad*)

entries.related: *a one-hit wonder* — an artist known for only one success; *a fad* — a short-lived trend; *here to stay* — lasting, the opposite.
entries.origin: From old flintlock guns, where the gunpowder in the pan could flash without firing the shot.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Ordinary and not special in any way.
entries.usage: Used, often slightly critically, about products, places, jobs and performances. It's most often used before a noun, where it's hyphenated: *a run-of-the-mill hotel*. In the negative it becomes praise: *This is no run-of-the-mill pizza place.*
examples: We stayed at a **run-of-the-mill** motel off the highway; it was clean and cheap.
This is no **run-of-the-mill** pizza place — they make their own mozzarella every morning.
My job is pretty **run-of-the-mill**: emails, meetings and a lot of spreadsheets.

drill.sentence: The movie wasn't terrible, but it was a pretty {{run-of-the-mill}} action film with the usual car chases.
drill.hint: ordinary and unremarkable (a factory image)

entries.related: *garden-variety* — ordinary, American; *nothing to write home about* — not very good or special; *one of a kind* — unique, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start something that causes many new problems that you did not expect and cannot easily stop.
entries.usage: Common in news, policy discussion and serious conversation, usually as a warning: *That would open Pandora's box.* It's neutral to formal, and *open a Pandora's box* is also common. It also works as a noun phrase: *The new rule could be a Pandora's box.*
examples: If we change the rules for one family, we'll **open Pandora's box**, and every parent will want an exception.
Asking my uncle why he left the family business **opened a Pandora's box** of old grudges.
Some experts warn that editing human genes could **open Pandora's box**.

drill.sentence: Our lawyer warned that suing the neighbors over the tree could {{open Pandora's box}}, leading to years of expensive fights over the property line.
drill.hint: start a chain of trouble that can't be stopped — a Greek myth (not *a can of worms*)

entries.related: *open a can of worms* — start a complicated, unpleasant situation, more informal; *a slippery slope* — one step that leads to worse ones; *open the floodgates* — allow something to happen on a huge scale.
entries.origin: From Greek myth: Pandora opened a jar, later described as a box, and released all the evils into the world.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take a big risk and stop worrying about the possible dangers.
entries.usage: Used about bold or impulsive decisions, often with approval or humor: *We threw caution to the wind and booked the trip.* It's neutral and slightly dramatic. *Throw caution to the winds* is also used.
examples: We **threw caution to the wind** and spent our savings on a trip around the world.
On the last night of our vacation, we **threw caution to the wind** and ordered every dessert on the menu.
During the housing boom, many buyers **threw caution to the wind** and took on loans they couldn't afford.

drill.sentence: After years of playing it safe, Rosa {{threw caution to the wind}} and moved to Paris without a job lined up.
drill.hint: stopped worrying about the risks (not *took the plunge*)

entries.related: *take the plunge* — finally do something risky or important; *roll the dice* — take a chance; *play it safe* — avoid risks, the opposite.
